subject: English
description: Affirmative ↔ negative, simple ↔ complex, degrees of comparison, exclamatory ↔ assertive

questions.stem: Choose the correct affirmative form of: 'No man is happy without health.'

options.option_text: Every man without health is happy.
Every man with health is happy.
All men are unhappy with health.
Some men are happy without health.

questions.explanation: Negative ('No man... without...') has TWO negatives — they cancel out. So the statement means 'Every man WITH health is happy'. Rule for double-negation: 'No X is Y without Z' ≡ 'Every X with Z is Y'. Useful related transformations — 'None but X' ≡ 'Only X', 'Not less than' ≡ 'At least'.

questions.stem: Transform into a complex sentence: 'I know his address.'

options.option_text: I know his address and his phone number.
I know where he lives.
Knowing his address, I called him.
His address is known to me.

questions.explanation: Complex sentence = 1 main clause + 1+ subordinate clauses joined by subordinating conjunctions (where, when, that, because, although, if, since…). 'I know his address' (simple) → 'I know where he lives' (complex — subordinate noun clause 'where he lives'). Compound = two independent clauses joined by FANBOYS (and, but, or…).

questions.stem: Transform 'Mumbai is the largest city in India' into a comparative degree sentence.

options.option_text: Mumbai is as large as any other city in India.
Mumbai is larger than any other city in India.
No city in India is large.
Mumbai is large like other cities in India.

questions.explanation: Three degrees of comparison: positive ('No other city in India is AS LARGE AS Mumbai'); comparative ('Mumbai is LARGER THAN ANY OTHER city in India'); superlative ('Mumbai is THE LARGEST city in India'). Note 'any OTHER' is essential when comparing within a group — without 'other', a thing would be compared to itself.

questions.stem: Transform 'How beautifully she sings!' into an assertive (declarative) sentence.

options.option_text: She does not sing well.
She sings very beautifully.
She is beautiful when she sings.
She is a beautiful singer.

questions.explanation: Exclamatory → Assertive: replace 'How / What a' with 'very' (or 'so / extremely') + drop the exclamation mark + adjust word order to subject-verb-rest. 'How beautifully she sings!' → 'She sings very beautifully.' Other examples: 'What a fool he is!' → 'He is a great fool.' 'How tall the building is!' → 'The building is very tall.'

questions.stem: Choose the correct interrogative form of: 'Everybody likes ice-cream.'

options.option_text: Does everybody like ice-cream?
Who does not like ice-cream?
Why does everybody like ice-cream?
How is ice-cream liked?

questions.explanation: An assertive sentence with universal quantifier ('everybody', 'no one') is best transformed into a rhetorical question of OPPOSITE polarity. 'Everybody likes' (positive universal) → 'Who does NOT like?' (negative interrogative — same meaning). Conversely 'No one likes' → 'Who likes?'. Direct 'Does everybody like?' shifts the meaning to a yes/no inquiry, not the universal claim.

questions.stem: Transform 'As soon as he saw the police, he ran away.' to start with 'No sooner...'

options.option_text: No sooner did he see the police than he ran away.
No sooner he saw the police than he ran away.
No sooner he had seen the police, then he ran away.
No sooner he saw the police but he ran away.

questions.explanation: Standard 'No sooner ... than ...' construction requires AUXILIARY INVERSION + 'than' (NOT 'then'). 'No sooner DID he see the police THAN he ran away.' Common errors: forgetting the inversion ('No sooner he saw' is wrong); using 'when' or 'but' instead of 'than'; using 'then' (a temporal adverb) instead of 'than' (a comparison conjunction).

questions.stem: Pick the correct passive form: 'They will finish the project tomorrow.'

options.option_text: The project will finish tomorrow.
The project will be finished by them tomorrow.
The project is finished tomorrow.
The project has been finished tomorrow.

questions.explanation: Future Indefinite passive: subject + will be + V3 (past participle) + by + agent. 'They will finish' → 'will be finished'. Object 'project' becomes new subject; the doer 'they' becomes 'by them' (often dropped if obvious). Future Continuous passive doesn't exist in standard usage. Future Perfect: 'will have finished' → 'will have been finished'.
